description.en: Fifteen centuries of roads between China and the Mediterranean: envoys and monks, silk and paper, Marco Polo and the plague — and how sea routes took over from the caravans.

title.en: Zhang Qian's mission to the West

text.en: Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian to seek allies against the Xiongnu. After years in captivity he reached Ferghana and Bactria and returned with knowledge of the western lands.

title.en: Gan Ying turns back from Rome

text.en: General Ban Chao sent Gan Ying to Rome. He reached the 'western sea', where Parthian sailors told him the voyage could take two years and travellers carried three years' supplies.

title.en: Cai Lun and the invention of paper

text.en: The court eunuch Cai Lun presented the Han emperor with a method of making paper from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets. The cheap, light material replaced bamboo slips and silk, and later spread through the Islamic world to Europe.

Byzantium paid dearly for silk and even believed it came from India. Around 552 two monks promised Justinian they would fetch silkworms, and returned from Asia with eggs hidden in their bamboo canes — the start of the empire's own silk industry.

In 629 the monk Xuanzang slipped out of Chang'an against the emperor's ban and travelled through Central Asia to India. He studied at Nalanda, toured almost the whole subcontinent and returned in 645 with 657 Buddhist texts, which he spent the rest of his life translating.

An Abbasid army defeated Tang Chinese forces by the Talas River in Central Asia. The battle secured Islamic influence in the region, and according to tradition captured Chinese artisans brought the secret of papermaking to Samarkand.

Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris: the Round City, named Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Baghdad quickly grew into one of the world's largest cities and a centre of Islamic science, trade and culture.

The Mongol army of Hulagu stormed and sacked Baghdad, and the last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim, was executed. The destruction of the caliphal capital and its libraries symbolically ended the Islamic Golden Age.

The Venetian Marco Polo travelled to China with his father and uncle and spent some 17 years at the court of Kublai Khan. His book of travels became Europe's chief source of knowledge about Asia for centuries.

Genoese galleys from Caffa brought plague to Messina in Sicily, from where it swept across Europe. Within a few years the Black Death killed an estimated third to half of the continent's population, reshaping its economy and society.

Admiral Zheng He's fleet of hundreds of ships made seven voyages across the Indian Ocean, reaching Arabia and the East African coast. The expeditions displayed Ming power, but the court halted them after 1433.

Vasco da Gama's Portuguese squadron sailed around Africa and reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast. Opening the sea route to India launched direct European maritime trade with Asia and European colonial expansion.
